what: GLM-GPU-DEMO-03 dyad review of the GPU-driven membrane demo

camera.note: camera POSTed to /camera before /frame; oblique view, phi 0.7 rad above the rim plane; engine world y-up

render.mode: fill + edge-contrast wire pass (GLM-GPU-DEMO-EDGE-01: the demo instance latched CHIMERA_MD_EDGE at init; demo-scoped, mesh_mode_ untouched; verified against the fill-only run by byte-differing PNGs and identical accepted_state_id values)
render.presentation: rigid B2(z-up)->engine(y-up) rotation plus a 0.5 m presentation lift; the lift is render presentation only

raised.note: centre raised 0.125 m over a 1.0 m rim radius

relaxed.note: GPU-relaxed; CPU law terminal energy 2.5980761647224426 J; centre height ~0 m

physical_briefing:
This object is six triangles joined around one centre vertex. The six outer vertices are fixed in a flat hexagonal rim. The centre can move only perpendicular to the rim plane.

Its energy is U = gamma x total triangle area. Forces are the negative gradient of that energy. For positive gamma, the optimizer seeks less area, so the raised centre approaches the rim plane. At gamma=0 this model produces no force, so the initial bump remains.

This is an area-minimization experiment. It contains no certified elasticity, bending stiffness, water pressure, gravity or contact dynamics. Optimization iterations are not physical time.

At identical geometry, doubling gamma doubles calculated energy and force; that alone does not require a visible shape change.

calls.label: gpu_demo_raised_gamma0
calls.report:
**1. What is actually visible.** The frame splits into two flat colour bands with a hard horizontal seam at roughly 43 % of the height: a saturated blue band on top (background/clear‑colour, no gradient) and a dark charcoal‑grey band below (the floor plane). There are **no grid lines, no scale marks, no HUD/text**, and no other objects. Centred on the seam is a single hexagonal silhouette that straddles the horizon: its upper part (against the blue) reads as a flat darker‑blue fill, its lower part (on the grey floor) as a flat dark‑grey fill with faintly lighter edge outlines forming the six sides. Near the top of this hexagon there is a thin, bright horizontal "lens/eye" sliver (pale yellow‑white) with two pale cyan lines flaring out to the left and right tips — i.e. an edge‑contrast/wire highlight on the upper rim and the two side vertices. That is all: one hexagon + a thin lit top edge, on a two‑tone empty scene.

**2. Locating centre vs rim.** The **outer rim** is reasonably locatable as the six‑corner hexagonal outline (the widest left/right points where the cyan spikes end, and the top/bottom corners of the grey body). The **centre vertex** I *cannot* locate with confidence: there is no distinct bright apex sitting clearly above the middle of the hexagon. The brightest point lies along the upper edge / back‑rim region rather than as a separate raised node, so "where exactly the centre is" is ambiguous from pixels alone.

**3. Resolvable? — *uncertain* (leaning not resolvable).** I can see the membrane is not a tall cone and that there is at most a very thin vertical extent above the rim outline, but the apparent separation between any raised centre and the rim plane is only a few pixels — comparable to the wire‑pass line thickness and anti‑aliasing. With no grid or scale reference and an oblique (φ≈0.7 rad) view that foreshortens height, I cannot confidently resolve or measure a 0.125 m offset; it is at or below what this image lets me distinguish from "flat".

**4. Consistent / inconsistent / can't tell — *consistent in the weak sense, but the specific height is not visually confirmable*.** Nothing in the image contradicts a shallow raised hexagon: there is no deep cone, no exploded/relaxed‑flat disc with zero thickness that would obviously contradict the "raised 0.125 m" label, and the thin lit top band is plausibly the upper triangle faces of a small bump. However, because the bump is not clearly separated from the rim (see Q3), I also cannot visually rule out that it looks essentially flat — which would be the relaxed appearance. So: no visible inconsistency, but the *magnitude* of the raise is not independently verifiable from this single oblique frame.

**5. What could explain apparent discrepancies + needed evidence.** The thinness/flat look can be explained by (a) the shallow 0.125 m‑over‑1 m ratio producing only a few pixels of vertical separation at cam_radius 6; (b) the oblique φ=0.7 view compressing height; (c) the fill + edge‑contrast wire pass putting a bright highlight on the top rim that masks any small apex; and (d) the render‑only +0.5 m presentation lift shifting where the rim projects relative to the floor horizon, which is what makes the hexagon straddle the seam in two tones. To distinguish raised‑from‑flat I would want: an orthographic **top view** (apex offset becomes a clear radial displacement), a **side/edge‑on view with a vertical scale bar or grid**, and a side‑by‑side of this frame vs the *relaxed* state at identical camera so the difference in top‑band thickness is directly comparable.

**6. Single worst visual problem.** The centre offset — the entire point of this "initial‑height" state — is **not visually legible**: the object renders as a near‑flat hexagon with only a thin lit edge, and there is **no grid/scale reference**, so a viewer cannot see or measure that the centre is raised 0.125 m above the rim plane. (Secondary issues: very low contrast of the grey body against the dark floor, and the two‑tone split at the horizon making it hard to tell which faces are "up".)

*Caveat throughout:* I am reading a single still with no pixel ruler; exact vertex positions, the true vertical separation, and whether the bright sliver is a raised apex vs. a rim edge‑highlight are all judged by eye and remain uncertain.

calls.label: gpu_demo_final_relaxed
calls.report:
**1. What is visibly distinguishable**
The frame is dominated by two flat, uniform bands split by a sharp horizontal line at roughly the vertical middle: a bright, saturated blue upper region (sky/background) and a dark‑gray lower region (floor/ground). There are no grid lines on the floor, no other panels, props, or scene content. Thin black bars run along the very top and bottom edges (viewport border / letterbox, not scene geometry). In the horizontal centre sits a single flat, regular‑hexagon‑shaped dark patch that straddles the horizon line: its top edge lies above the line, its leftmost and rightmost vertices sit near the line, and its bottom edge lies below it. The fill of this hexagon is two‑toned — a darker blue than the sky where it overlaps the upper band, and a near‑black gray only slightly lighter than the floor where it overlaps the lower band. I do **not** see bright wireframe lines or internal spokes; the hexagon's outline is defined purely by color difference against the background.

**2. Locating centre vertex and outer rim**
The *outer rim* (the six fixed vertices) is locatable: it is the boundary where the dark fill meets the sky/floor — top horizontal edge above the horizon, left/right extreme vertices at the horizon, bottom horizontal edge below. The *centre vertex* is **not directly visible**: there is no dot, marker, or set of converging spokes to pin it down. It can only be *inferred* as the geometric centre of the hexagon (the point where the six triangles meet). So: rim = seen by outline; centre = inferred, not observed.

**3. Is the centre's offset resolvable?**
**Not resolvable.** The shape reads as flat — there is no visible central peak or shallow pyramid — which is qualitatively consistent with a height of ~0 m. But in this oblique view, at this small on‑screen size and with no side/edge‑on reference or scale bar, I cannot distinguish "exactly zero" from "a tiny residual bump." So the offset is not visually measurable; all I can say is "no obvious bump present."

**4. Consistent / inconsistent / cannot tell?**
**Consistent**, with caveats. A flat, un‑bumped hexagon matches the stated relaxed/stagnated state (centre height ~0 m); nothing in the image contradicts that. Caveats: I cannot independently confirm exact flatness or the recorded energy from pixels alone, and the described *edge‑contrast wire pass* is not clearly visible as distinct lines to me — only color boundaries are. So the "flat hexagon" reading is consistent with the state, but the wire‑pass portion of the render description is not visually confirmed by this image.

**5. Could viewpoint/occlusion/lighting/rendering explain discrepancies? What extra evidence would help?**
Yes. (a) The oblique camera foreshortens vertical displacement, so a small residual height would be sub‑pixel and invisible. (b) The two‑tone fill split exactly at the horizon is most plausibly background showing through a dark/translucent face (blue sky vs gray floor) or a clipping artifact at the floor's far edge — not real geometry; I cannot judge which from this image. (c) The missing visible wires are likely a low‑contrast wire color plus flat, unlit shading (no lighting model), so facet structure doesn't show. Distinguishing evidence: an orthographic top‑down view, an edge‑on/side view to read height directly, a high‑contrast wire pass or explicit vertex markers (especially at the centre), a side‑by‑side with the *raised* state for scale, and/or an on‑screen numeric readout of centre height.

**6. Single worst visual problem**
The membrane's defining structure is not legible: there are no visible triangle edges, no spokes, and no marker for the centre vertex, so the object reads only as a flat dark hexagon patch with an unexplained horizontal color split (the two‑tone horizon line) that looks like a rendering artifact. In short, poor fill/background contrast plus the absent wireframe make it hard to confirm what is actually being rendered — you cannot see the six‑triangle fan or its centre at all.
